issues.legal_issue: A state legislature cannot regulate mining leases for minor minerals in a field that parliamentary legislation has taken under central control.
material_facts: The leases concerned quarrying minor minerals and were granted before the state amendment and rules at issue.

After the central statute declared that the Union would control mine regulation and mineral development to the extent provided in that statute, it provided that state governments could make rules regulating the grant of prospecting licences and mining leases for minor minerals and for connected purposes.
The state amended its land-reform statute to substitute terms of existing minor-mineral leases that conflicted with state rules.
issues.conclusion: The state amendment was beyond the state legislature’s competence and invalid because parliamentary legislation had covered the relevant field of minor-mineral regulation.
issues.legal_principle: Under Constitution, Seventh Schedule, List I Entry 54 and List II Entry 23, a parliamentary declaration under section 2 of the Mines and Minerals (Regulation and Development) Act, 1957 withdraws from the states the legislative field covered by that Act. Sections 14 and 15 address minor minerals and place regulation of the grant of their prospecting licences and mining leases, and connected purposes, within the statutory scheme. The Court applied Hingir-Rampur Coal Co. Ltd. v. State of Orissa and State of Orissa v. M.A. Tulloch & Co. It rejected the argument that the amendment was principally about land and land tenures: once mining leases exist, their regulation falls under the mining entry, even if it incidentally affects land; parliamentary control also counts as control by the Union.

rule.if: constitutional_validity_challenge and minor_mineral_lease_regulation and parliamentary_law_covers_the_field and state_law_regulates_existing_leases

predicates.constitutional_validity_challenge: A party challenges the constitutional validity of a state law in a proceeding concerning mining leases.
predicates.minor_mineral_lease_regulation: The challenged law regulates leases for the extraction of minor minerals.
predicates.parliamentary_law_covers_the_field: Parliamentary legislation has taken under central control the field that the challenged law regulates.
predicates.state_law_regulates_existing_leases: The state law changes or governs the terms of existing mining leases.

issues.definition: When a constitutional challenge concerns state regulation of existing minor-mineral leases in a field covered by parliamentary legislation, the state law is invalid.

issues.legal_issue: A state-made rule cannot alter the terms of existing mining leases without legislative authority from a competent legislature.
material_facts: The leases were granted before the state rules were made and remained in force when the rules were amended.
The amended rule purported to apply rent, royalty, and surface-rent terms to leases that already existed.

The parliamentary statute authorized modification of certain earlier leases but did not provide authority to alter leases of minor minerals granted after the specified cutoff; Parliament had not enacted a provision authorizing alteration of the leases at issue.
The state amendment that purported to authorize substitution of existing lease terms was invalid.
issues.conclusion: The amended rule was ineffective to alter the terms of the existing leases because it lacked support from a competent legislative enactment.
issues.legal_principle: Vested interests cannot be taken away except under authority of law; rule-making power alone is insufficient. Sections 15 and 16 of the Mines and Minerals (Regulation and Development) Act, 1957 did not authorize the state rule to alter existing leases of the kind at issue: section 15 concerned rules regulating the grant of leases and connected purposes, while section 16 provided for modification only of leases granted before its specified cutoff. The Court also relied on the principle, applied in Hingir-Rampur Coal Co. Ltd. v. State of Orissa and State of Orissa v. M.A. Tulloch & Co., that the parliamentary legislation had withdrawn the relevant minor-mineral field from state legislative competence.

rule.if: challenge_to_subordinate_rule and existing_mining_lease_predates_rule and rule_purports_to_change_lease_terms and no_competent_legislative_authority_for_change

predicates.challenge_to_subordinate_rule: A party challenges a subordinate rule in a proceeding concerning a mining lease.
predicates.existing_mining_lease_predates_rule: The mining lease was already in force before the challenged rule was made.
predicates.rule_purports_to_change_lease_terms: The rule purports to apply new terms to a lease that already existed.
predicates.no_competent_legislative_authority_for_c: No enactment by a legislature competent to legislate on the subject authorizes the rule to change the terms of that existing lease.

issues.definition: If a challenged rule purports to change a pre-existing mining lease and no competent legislative enactment authorizes that change, the rule cannot change the lease terms.
